summary: Defines the DHCP Relay Agent Information option, which lets a relay add details such as where a request came from before passing it to a server. Operators of shared access networks can use this to apply their own policies and protect against some abuse. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3046 lets a DHCP relay add information about where a request came from. A server can use that information when assigning addresses or other settings.

subtitle: A DHCP option that lets a relay add trusted circuit or subscriber information to a request.

tldr.problem: On shared access networks, a DHCP server may not know which circuit or remote host sent a request. Client-supplied identifiers can be spoofed.
tldr.mechanism: A relay adds a Relay Agent Information option with sub-options such as circuit ID and remote ID. A supporting server echoes the option, and the relay removes it before forwarding the response to the client.
tldr.outcome: Servers can use the relay-supplied information for address and parameter policies, assuming the relay, server, and network between them are trusted. RFC 3046 has been updated by RFC 6607.

today: RFC 3046 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6607.

sections.title: The Problem on Shared Access Networks
sections.content:
In some public access networks, circuit access equipment connects many customer hosts to a central DHCP server. The equipment acts as a router and DHCP relay. Without additional information, the server may not know which circuit or modem originated a request.

The RFC describes risks including address exhaustion and spoofing of client identifiers or MAC addresses. Its approach is for the trusted access equipment to add information to client-originated DHCP requests before forwarding them to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP server may receive requests from many customer circuits without knowing which circuit sent each one. A relay can add information that identifies the request's source circuit.

sections.title: The Relay Agent Information Option
sections.content:
RFC 3046 defines DHCP option 82 as a container for one or more sub-options. Each sub-option has a code, a length, and a value. The first two sub-options are Agent Circuit ID (code 1) and Agent Remote ID (code 2).

The outer length counts the bytes of all sub-option tuples, and each sub-option length counts only its value. At least one sub-option is required, making the minimum option length two. The option has no pad sub-option and must not end with sub-option code 255.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 82 carries smaller fields that describe the request's circuit or remote endpoint. Each field includes its own type and length.

sections.title: How the Relay Adds and Removes the Option
sections.content:
Adding the option should be configurable and disabled by default. When a relay adds it to a client-to-server BOOTP or DHCP packet, it places it last in the options field, before the End option if present. A relay receiving an already-tagged packet from an untrusted first-hop circuit discards it and increments an error count.

A supporting server echoes the entire option in its replies. The relay or trusted downstream element that added the option removes it before forwarding the server response to the client. The relay must not modify packets that use IPsec Authentication Header or Encapsulating Security Payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay adds the option to the request, and the server copies it into its reply. The relay removes it before sending the reply to the client.

sections.title: Circuit ID and Remote ID
sections.content:
The Agent Circuit ID is an identifier local to the relay for the circuit where the request arrived. Examples in the RFC include a router interface, a switch port, or a virtual circuit number. A server may use it for address or parameter policy and should treat it as an opaque value rather than parse it.

The Agent Remote ID identifies the remote end of a circuit, such as a modem or user. It must be globally unique. A server may use it to select settings for a user, host, or modem, and the relay may use it when choosing the circuit for a reply.
sections.plainLanguage: The circuit ID identifies the access circuit at the relay. The remote ID identifies the user or device at the other end of that circuit.

sections.title: Trust Assumptions and Status Today
sections.content:
The security model treats clients as untrusted and assumes that the relay, DHCP server, and network between them are trusted and secure. The option can support policies that limit address assignments or associate addresses with a remote ID, but the RFC does not define cryptographic authentication of that ID. It encourages such authentication to be considered.

RFC 3046 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6607. The option's protection depends on DHCP traffic from public hosts passing through the relay and on the relay-to-server network remaining uncompromised.
sections.plainLanguage: The server must be able to trust the relay's information. This option does not itself authenticate the relay or the remote ID cryptographically.
